Introduction · Renewable Energy

What Is Renewable Energy?

1Renewable energy

Solar, wind, and hydropower. Renewable energy comes from sources that are replenished naturally.

SolarWindHydropower
2Energy transition

Shifting energy systems toward lower-carbon alternatives.

1990 · 0.03%wind + solar, world electricity17.3% · 2025
3Intermittency

A major challenge of renewable energy is the intermittency of some energy sources, such as solar and wind.

Wind and solar’s share of the world’s electricity: Ember (2026), via Our World in Data. The one-day output sketch is illustrative.

Introduction · Comparing Energy Sources

Energy Return on Investment (EROI)

EROI stands for Energy Return on Investment.

energy deliveredenergy invested to get it

A high EROI indicates that more energy is gained than expended to obtain it.

Out of every 100 units of energy delivered…
spent getting energyleft for society

Approximate harmonized EROIs read from Murphy, Raugei, Carbajales-Dale & Rubio Estrada (2022), “Energy Return on Investment of Major Energy Carriers: Review and Harmonization,” Sustainability 14:7098, Figure 7 (electricity, primary-energy equivalent in a thermal-dominated grid) and Section 3.2.1 (oil as a fuel at the point of use). Electricity and a liquid fuel are different energy products, and these are review estimates under one set of assumptions, not fixed constants of each technology.

Introduction · Comparing Energy Sources

Impacts of Power Plants

Every power plant has costs that are not on the electric bill. Press Tour the five plants.
Powering a city of 1 million people for one year

Hidden costs: medians of published estimates for each source, mostly global and historical, Sovacool, Kim & Yang (2021), Energy Research & Social Science 72:101885, Table 1 (US$2018). Deaths from accidents and air pollution, historical rates: Markandya & Wilkinson (2007), The Lancet, and Sovacool et al. (2016), Journal of Cleaner Production, via Our World in Data (2021). City: 13 TWh a year (U.S. generation per person, Ember 2025, × 1 million). The two measures come from different studies and methods; scaling them to one city is an illustration, not a forecast for any real U.S. city.

The Carbon Footprint of Electricity

Definition

The process of reducing carbon emissions from energy, transportation, and industry is known as decarbonization.

Which strategy supports decarbonization?

Improving energy efficiency and renewable energy use.

Try it: one U.S. home’s electricity for a year
tonnes CO₂e a year

Grid: Ember U.S. 2025 mix weighted by the same medians, about 346 g/kWh; with wind and solar in place of coal and gas, about 25 g/kWh.

14.1 · Solar Power

Three Ways to Capture the Sun

The National Renewable Energy Laboratory estimates that 14 million acres of solar panels, roughly the size of Lake Michigan, could generate as much electricity as the United States uses in a year.

Advantages

  • Freely available and nondepletable
  • No combustion emissions
  • Rapidly deployable on rooftops, parking lots and fields
  • Rooftop collectors also heat water stored in tanks, cutting water-heating costs

Challenges

  • Needs consistent sunlight: output varies with weather and time of day, so storage is needed
  • Mining the minerals in panels carries its own environmental trade-offs

Denholm & Margolis (2008), Energy Policy 36:3531, summarized by NREL: about 181 m² of PV per person to meet U.S. electricity demand (mid-2000s demand and panels), about 0.6% of U.S. land. An annual energy match, not a design for round-the-clock supply: storage and transmission are not included. Lake Michigan outline: Natural Earth 1:50m (about 58,000 km²), drawn to the same scale as a 14-million-acre square (56,700 km²).

14.2 · Hydropower

Water Power: 6% of Global Energy

⟶⟶⟶⟶⟶
0 MW

Power = water’s weight × drop × flow × efficiency

How it works

Flowing water spins turbines. Dams store water; run-of-river systems use the natural flow without large reservoirs.

Advantages

Can be dispatched on demand within water limits (reservoirs store water to shift generation), no combustion emissions, and a long operating life. Output still depends on rain, snowmelt and drought.

Trade-offs

1Fish migration blocked 2sediment trapped 3flooded vegetation releases methane 4communities displaced: Three Gorges Dam displaced over 1 million people.

Illustrative dam: head 60–180 m, flow up to 800 m³/s, 90% efficiency. Homes assume about 10,500 kWh a year per U.S. home (EIA).

14.2 · Nuclear Power

Nuclear Fission

800 MW

ChernobylUkraine (then the Soviet Union) · April 26, 1986

A flawed reactor design and an unsafe test triggered a steam explosion and fire that spread radioactive material across Europe.

Fukushima DaiichiJapan · March 11, 2011

An earthquake and the tsunami it caused knocked out power to the cooling systems, and three reactors melted down.

Pellet comparison: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Nuclear Energy. U.S. share: about 9% of primary energy and 19% of electricity (EIA). Plant: a simplified pressurized-water reactor; a typical U.S. reactor makes about 1,000 MW.

14.2 · Geothermal Energy

Geothermal Energy

Location-dependent: the best resources are in Iceland, New Zealand, and parts of the U.S. West, where hot rock lies close to the surface.

Ground temperature at depth: about 10–16°C (50–60°F) in much of the U.S. (U.S. DOE, Energy Saver, “Geothermal Heat Pumps”). Map: Natural Earth.

14.4 · Energy Conservation

Using Less Energy

Energy efficiency means using less energy to achieve the same result.

Example: a fuel-efficient vehicle travels the same distance using less fuel.

0 W idle · 0 kWh a year · $0 a year
23%of household electricity went to always-on, idle devices in a study of about 70,000 Northern California homes: 164 watts around the clock.NRDC, 2015
$19 billiona year nationwide (2015 estimate of all idle use, not all of it avoidable), about $165 per household: the output of 50 large power plants.NRDC, 2015
23%of projected 2020 U.S. energy demand outside transportation could be avoided: about $1.2 trillion in gross savings for about $520 billion invested.McKinsey & Company, 2009
Beyond the homeSmart grids use sensors and controls to cut waste; higher-voltage lines lose less of the roughly 5% of power lost in transmission and distribution.U.S. EIA

NRDC (2015), Home Idle Load (Delforge, Schmidt & Schmidt; Stanford Sustainable Systems Lab data). McKinsey & Company (2009), Unlocking Energy Efficiency in the U.S. Economy (savings are the 2009–2020 total). Device idle draws: typical values from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory standby measurements; yours will vary. 17¢/kWh (EIA).

14.5 · Transition Drivers

What Could Drive a Transition Away from Fossil Fuels?

I

Falling Costs

The cost of wind and solar has fallen steadily for decades. Solar jobs now greatly outnumber coal jobs and economics are decisively shifting.

II

Government Policy

R&D funding, tax incentives, and utility purchase mandates have driven wind and solar growth in Texas, Iowa, California, and Arizona.

DSIRE: every state incentive ↗
III

The Solutions Project

Stanford/UC Berkeley researchers mapped how all 50 US states could transition to 100% renewable energy by 2050 using available technology.

IV

Grid & Storage Innovation

Smart grids, microgrids, and V2G technology improve resilience and allow variable wind and solar to reliably meet demand.

Solar module prices (the panels only, not the installed cost of a system): IRENA (2025) and other sources, via Our World in Data (constant 2025 US$ per watt). Jobs, 2024: about 370,600 in solar power vs. about 124,800 in coal mining and coal power (U.S. DOE, 2025 U.S. Energy and Employment Report). The Solutions Project roadmap is a modeled scenario (Jacobson et al., 2015), not a forecast. State shares: Ember, US Electricity Data (wind and solar share of each state’s electricity generation, 2025).

14.5 · The Transition · Simulator

Renewable Energy Simulator

Presets
day 2 is cloudy; on day 3 the wind nearly stops
Generation vs. demandsolarwindbatterygascoaldemand
–renewable
–CO₂ emitted
–blackout hours
–curtailed (wasted)

Set the grid, then run a day. Solar and wind generate when nature allows; the battery stores the surplus; gas and coal fill the gaps. Can you reach 100% renewable without a blackout?

Illustrative regional grid (demand peaks near 104 GW). Dispatch: renewables first, then the battery (90% round trip, discharge limited to capacity ÷ 4 h), then gas and coal in proportion to capacity. The battery charges only from surplus wind and solar, after a warm-up run of the same period that starts it empty. Fixed weather days, not a year of real weather, so a run cannot show year-round reliability. CO₂: about 0.45 t/MWh gas, 0.95 t/MWh coal (EPA, EIA).

Simulation Results · Simulations

Simulations: 350-mile range EV

Selected example months, not probabilities. Each month runs 31 days from a full battery: daily miles are drawn at random (the EV Charging Calculator’s negative-binomial model), the car charges overnight at home on Level 1, and whenever range reaches the 20-mile reserve a fast charge refills it. How often home charging falls short is what the calculator later in the deck estimates.

Chapter 14 · Key Concepts

Energy Alternatives: How Are Our Energy Decisions Changing?

Renewable Energy
Energy from sources that are replenished naturally: sun, wind and flowing water
Energy Transition
Shifting energy systems toward lower-carbon alternatives
Intermittency
Solar and wind output rises and falls with the weather and the time of day
EROI
Energy Return on Investment: energy delivered for each unit of energy spent getting it
Externalities
Hidden costs, such as pollution and health harms, paid by society rather than on the bill
Decarbonization
Reducing carbon emissions from energy, transportation and industry
Energy Efficiency
Using less energy to achieve the same result
Photovoltaic (PV) Panel
Silicon panel producing electricity when exposed to sunlight
Hydropower
Falling water spins turbines: about 14% of the world’s electricity (2025); ecosystem trade-offs
Nuclear Fission
Splitting uranium nuclei to generate heat and electricity
NIMBY
“Not In My Back Yard”: supporting a project, but not near home
EV and V2G
Electric vehicles; vehicle-to-grid lets parked EV batteries supply power back to the grid
